rows.selection_reason: With no prior experiments, the most critical uncertainty is whether each modality individually carries sufficient signal for the classification task, and what performance floor we should expect. Config_005 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) is the simplest, cleanest baseline: it uses a well-established RNA encoder (scgpt), the simplest profile setting, and no image processing or fusion. Establishing the RNA-only performance first provides an essential reference point against which all subsequent image-only and multimodal results can be meaningfully compared. Without this baseline, a multimodal result would be uninterpretable—we could not tell whether fusion is adding value or merely matching a strong single-modality model. This experiment is also computationally lightweight, conserving budget for the multimodal experiments that follow.

We have a single baseline (config_005: rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt → acc 0.411, F1 0.378), leaving major uncertainty about whether the image modality contributes any predictive signal. config_027 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, no aggregation, concat fusion) is the minimal structural change from config_005: it keeps the same RNA encoder (scgpt), the same profile setting (singleprofile), and adds only the image branch with a simple concat fusion (which is structurally necessary once a second modality is present). This directly isolates the effect of adding image information. If config_027 substantially exceeds 0.411, image adds value and we can then explore which image encoder, aggregation, or fusion strategy matters most. If it performs similarly or worse, we learn that the image modality (at least with this encoder/fusion) is not helping, redirecting budget toward RNA-side improvements (e.g., multiprofile, alternative encoders). Under a tight budget, resolving whether the second modality is worth pursuing is the highest-value uncertainty to reduce before committing experiments to finer-grained design choices.

Evidence: config_027 (multimodal, singleprofile, scgpt, imagenet_vit_l, concat) achieves 0.4348 acc / 0.4234 F1, outperforming config_005 (rna_only, singleprofile, scgpt) at 0.4106 acc / 0.3785 F1, indicating that adding image features with concat fusion is beneficial. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the fusion mechanism itself (concat vs. weighted) is a meaningful design choice, or whether the gain is purely from the additional modality. This experiment (config_051) is a clean single-variable change from config_027—only the fusion type shifts from concat to weighted—while holding RNA encoder (scgpt), image encoder (imagenet_vit_l), profile setting (singleprofile), and aggregation (None) constant. If weighted fusion improves performance, it reveals that modality weighting matters and guides future multiprofile/aggregation experiments; if it does not, concat is confirmed as sufficient and we can redirect budget toward testing aggregation or profile settings. This is the most informative next step under a limited budget because it isolates one important design axis from the current best configuration with minimal confounding.

Evidence: config_027 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, concat, singleprofile) is the best result so far (acc=0.4348, F1=0.4234), modestly outperforming RNA-only scgpt (config_005, acc=0.4106) and weighted-fusion multimodal (config_051, acc=0.4224). However, all three experiments used scgpt as the RNA encoder, so we have zero information about whether the RNA representation choice is a meaningful design axis. Question: config_021 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, concat, singleprofile) is a single-variable controlled comparison to config_027—only the RNA encoder changes from scgpt to scvi_n200. This isolates the effect of the RNA encoder while holding image encoder, fusion, and profile setting constant. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a tight budget, the RNA encoder is a fundamental design decision that could account for substantial performance variance. If scvi_n200 matches scgpt, we learn the RNA representation is not a bottleneck and can focus budget on other axes (aggregation, multiprofile, image encoder). If it differs substantially, we gain a critical design insight that reshapes the remaining search. This is more informative than, e.g., testing an image-only baseline or jumping to multiprofile, because it directly extends the strongest evidence we currently have with a minimal, interpretable change.

Evidence: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with concat fusion (config_021) achieved the best result so far (acc 0.532, F1 0.517), dramatically outperforming scgpt-based configs (~0.41–0.43). For scgpt, concat (0.435) slightly beat weighted (0.422), but the difference was small and the base performance was much lower. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether concat or weighted fusion is optimal when paired with the stronger scvi_n200 encoder—the fusion interaction may differ at higher representation quality. This experiment (config_006) tests exactly that: it changes only the fusion method (concat→weighted) while holding scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, and singleprofile fixed, giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_021. It is the best next use of budget because it is a low-risk, high-information exploitation step: if weighted matches or beats concat, it opens a new fusion direction; if concat remains superior, we confirm the best singleprofile multimodal recipe and can confidently move to testing multiprofile or alternative image encoders next.

All five completed experiments are singleprofile, so we have zero evidence on whether multiprofile (with aggregation) improves performance. The strongest finding is that scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l substantially outperforms scgpt-based configs (~0.53 vs ~0.42-0.43), and weighted fusion marginally edges concat for scvi_n200 (0.5375 vs 0.5321). Config_046 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) is the most direct multiprofile extension of our best singleprofile config (config_006), changing only the profile setting and adding the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates the effect of multiprofile while holding the RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion strategy constant. It is the highest-value next experiment because profile setting is the largest unexplored design axis, and knowing whether multiple profiles add signal (or just noise/complexity) will strongly guide all subsequent experiments involving aggregation and fusion.

Evidence: config_046 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) achieved the best accuracy (0.7062), a massive jump over the best singleprofile result (config_006, 0.5375). This confirms multiprofile is the dominant design lever. However, we have only one multiprofile data point, using avgpool aggregation. The key uncertainty is whether a more expressive aggregation (transformer) can further improve over simple average pooling when combining multiple profiles. Question: config_042 (transformer, weighted) isolates the aggregation method by changing only avgpool→transformer relative to config_046, keeping RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting, and fusion all identical. Why this is the best next experiment: Under a limited budget, understanding whether aggregation architecture matters is more informative than re-testing fusion (which showed negligible differences in singleprofile: config_006 vs config_021). If transformer aggregation yields a meaningful gain, it identifies a new optimization axis; if it does not, we can confidently conclude avgpool is sufficient and redirect budget toward other untested dimensions (e.g., image encoder choice or RNA encoder alternatives in the multiprofile setting).

Evidence: The current best configuration is config_042 (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1. In singleprofile settings, weighted fusion marginally outperformed concat (0.537 vs 0.532), but that difference was small. In the multiprofile regime—where performance gains are largest—we have only tested weighted fusion (config_042, config_046). The effect of fusion strategy in multiprofile is therefore untested. Question: config_013 is identical to config_042 except fusion changes from weighted to concat, isolating the fusion effect under the strongest-performing multiprofile + transformer aggregation setup. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable comparison against the current best, directly testing whether the fusion choice that showed only a marginal edge in singleprofile also matters (or even reverses) when multiprofile + transformer aggregation is in play. If concat matches or beats weighted, it broadens the design space at no cost; if weighted clearly wins, we confirm the fusion choice and can confidently move budget toward testing alternative RNA encoders or image encoders in the multiprofile setting. This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_042, acc=0.725) uses scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation and weighted fusion in the multiprofile setting. All completed multimodal experiments have exclusively used imagenet_vit_l as the image encoder, so the effect of the image encoder choice in the high-performing multiprofile regime is completely untested. Question: config_049 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) changes only the image encoder from imagenet_vit_l to resnet50, making it a clean single-variable comparison against config_042. This isolates whether the ViT-L backbone is essential or whether a simpler CNN (resnet50) could match or exceed it. Why this is the best use of the next budget: The image encoder is a major architectural decision that has been held constant across all 8 experiments. Under a limited budget, resolving whether this choice matters (and in which direction) is more informative than, e.g., re-testing fusion (weighted vs concat showed only ~0.004 difference) or testing a clearly inferior RNA encoder (scgpt was ~0.10 worse than scvi_n200 in singleprofile). A large gap would confirm imagenet_vit_l is critical; a small gap would free the search to focus on other axes.

Evidence: scvi_n200 clearly outperforms scgpt in singleprofile multimodal settings (~0.53 vs ~0.43 accuracy), and multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion is the strongest configuration (config_042: 0.725 acc). However, all multiprofile experiments so far use scvi_n200; we have zero data on how scgpt performs in the multiprofile regime. Uncertainty: it is unclear whether the aggregation step (transformer over multiple profiles) compensates for a weaker per-profile RNA representation, potentially narrowing or eliminating the scvi_n200 advantage. This experiment (config_001: scgpt, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_042, cleanly isolating the RNA encoder effect in the multiprofile regime. If scgpt is close to scvi_n200 here, it reveals that profile-level aggregation mitigates representation quality and opens a cheaper design space; if it is substantially worse, it confirms scvi_n200 is essential and we can focus remaining budget on image encoder and fusion refinements. This single-variable comparison is the highest-information experiment available under the limited budget.
